Students take readings of the volume of a liquid using three different pieces of measuring
equipment X, Y and Z.
The true value of the volume of the liquid is V.
The students’ results are shown.

hints: Notice the width of the number-of-readings curve for X, Y and Z - Y and Z are tall and narrow while X is broad and low.
Recall that precision is small random spread between readings, while accuracy is a mean value close to the true volume $V$ marked on each volume axis.
Check each peak centre against $V$ and each width separately, then count how many are narrow and how many are centred at $V$ to use the table.
walkthrough: Precision means repeated readings agree closely, shown by a narrow distribution. Accuracy means the mean reading is close to the true value $V$.
X has a broad spread centred at $V$, so its readings disagree but average to the true value - not precise but accurate.
Y has a very narrow peak centred well below $V$, so its readings agree but with a systematic shift - precise but not accurate.
Z has a very narrow peak centred at $V$, so its readings agree and average to the true value - both precise and accurate.
Counting gives precise pieces Y and Z, a total of 2, and accurate pieces X and Z, a total of 2. This is option D.

A.explanation: This undercounts both qualities because it misses that two distributions are narrow and two are centred at $V$.

B.explanation: This counts only one precise set, but both Y and Z show narrow tall peaks with small spread.

C.explanation: This counts only one accurate set, but both X and Z are centred on the true value $V$.

D.explanation: Y and Z are narrow so are precise, and X and Z are centred at $V$ so are accurate, giving 2 and 2.
